tier_reason: First-party numbers in the project's own PR descriptions (#419, #449, #451-#456) from public benchmark code (perf/graaflib/*_benchmark.cpp vs perf/boost/*_benchmark.cpp, Google Benchmark v1.8.2, Boost 1.84.0 tarball pinned in perf/CMakeLists.txt), but no CPU model, compiler version or flags beyond 'Release' are stated, so not A; every number shows Graaf slower than Boost.Graph.

corrections.caveats: FLAGGED NOT FASTER: every numeric comparison against the named baseline (Boost.Graph 1.84.0) shows Graaf slower, from 1.14x (Kruskal, web_google) to 17.01x (dijkstra_shortest_paths, web_berkstan); the README claims only a lightweight, easy-to-use alternative that 'doesn't sacrifice on performance'. The numbers are first-party PR descriptions with no hardware, no compiler version and no flags beyond 'Release' (the g++-12 and clang++-16 mentions refer to Debug test runs). The Boost comparison executable is opt-in (GRAAF_BUILD_BOOST_PERF, off by default); it uses boost::adjacency_list<vecS, vecS, undirectedS> and builds the graph outside the timed loop, as the Graaf benchmarks do, so the harness is like-for-like at a glance. The BFS gap figures in PR #449 do not match its own before/after timings: the implied Boost BFS time is about 672 ms before vs 374 ms after on web_google and about 229 ms vs 170 ms on web_berkstan (derived from page data), so the Boost reference was not stable between runs; the other PRs' gap ratios are internally consistent. PR #453 (dijkstra_shortest_path vector storage) was still open when read on 2026-10-07. Every perf PR in the series (#449, #451-#456) and the later commits carry a Claude co-author trailer (not only #454). The gaps are moving quickly (perf PRs merged 2026-09-19 to 2026-09-27, last commit 2026-09-28), so later commits may close more of the gap. Kept as a record only so the catalogue can show the evidence is negative. Category: graph-algorithms is not a spec category.

notes: Numbers all match the PRs (#419: Graaf 13.39 s vs Boost 1.33 s on web-Google, 14.11 s vs 0.69 s on web-BerkStan; latest gaps 1.14x-17.01x slower). Shortcomings to record: not faster than Boost.Graph on any algorithm; first-party, no CPU/compiler/flags; BFS gap in #449 inconsistent with its own timings; #453 unmerged. Category: no spec category fits a general graph-algorithms library; the nearest existing one is wave 8 sparse-and-solvers, which already holds graph-analytics entries (gunrock/graphblast, algebraic-programming/alp benchmarked on BFS/SSSP against SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS), but Graaf is a container-plus-algorithms library with Boost.Graph as its baseline, so either keep graph-algorithms as an off-spec category (baseline Boost Graph Library) or file it under sparse-and-solvers by override.

tier_reason: docs/perf.md gives only first-party llvm-mca static estimates (Skylake scheduling model) for two routines against GLM and RTM; the harness (perf/*_perf.cpp via mc_ruler) is public but compiler version and run-time measurements are absent, and the page itself says llvm-mca cannot predict performance, so C (numbers without measured methodology), not A or B.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated on the page. perf/CMakeLists.txt builds the analysed regions with mc_ruler (an llvm-mca harness that needs clang; version not stated) only in a Release build; the klein target adds -msse3; glm_perf.cpp uses GLM 0.9.9.7 (fetched by tag) with no GLM_FORCE_INTRINSICS or other GLM SIMD define and no -msse flag; RTM is fetched at origin/master.
corrections.hardware: No run-time hardware: llvm-mca static analysis with the Intel Skylake scheduling model (SKLPort0-7 resources, dispatch width 6) for every listing.
corrections.workload: Static llvm-mca analysis (100 iterations, dispatch width 6, Skylake model) of the compiled SSE assembly for two routines marked with mc_ruler MC_MEASURE regions in perf/klein_perf.cpp, perf/glm_perf.cpp and perf/rtm_perf.cpp: rotor (quaternion) composition and motor (dual-quaternion) application to a point; no run time is measured.
corrections.caveats: The only numbers are first-party llvm-mca cycle estimates; docs/perf.md itself says llvm-mca 'cannot be used as a proxy for predicting performance'. No run-time measurements are published: perf/ is the mc_ruler harness that produces these llvm-mca reports, not a timing benchmark. The GLM baseline is scalar: glm_perf.cpp defines no GLM_FORCE_INTRINSICS (GLM 0.9.9.7) and gets no -msse flag, and its listings are movss-based with stack spills, so GLM's own SIMD path was not used. The GLM motor routine converts the dual quaternion with glm::mat3x4_cast on every call, which inflates its count against Klein's direct motor-point application. Against RTM, the best SIMD baseline, rotor composition is a tie (821 vs 824 cycles), and no RTM motor routine is given. Compiler version unstated (mc_ruler requires clang). The project site jeremyong.com/klein is blocked here; the docs were read from the repo's docs/ folder. Repo archived on 2024-08-02 with the README saying it was paused for lack of time.

notes: Numbers match docs/perf.md exactly (rotor 821/2400 vs GLM 1522/5700 vs RTM 824/2300; motor 1831/5900 vs GLM 5435/14100; block RThroughput 8.0/14.0/7.0 and 13.5/38.5). Shortcomings to record: static llvm-mca estimates only, no measured run time; GLM baseline built without its SIMD path; GLM motor row includes a mat3x4_cast per call; ties RTM; archived.

tier_reason: Upgraded C to A: the third-party qlibs/mph perfect_hashing harness (benchmark branch, perfect_hashing/gperf.cpp and unordered_map.cpp with benchmark.hpp, Makefile, benchmark.ipynb) times gperf-generated lookup against std::unordered_map with public code, stated flags (-std=c++20 -DNDEBUG -O3 -march=native) and CPU (i7-12650H from /proc/cpuinfo in the notebook); the same page earned qlibs/mph its A in wave1-phf. Compiler labels (clang++-19, g++-13) are unreliable because the Makefile hard-codes CXX=clang++-18.

corrections.baseline: std::unordered_map<std::string_view, int> (std::hash in the perfect_hashing harness; boost::hash in the qlibs/mph README nanobench tables)
corrections.workload: qlibs/mph perfect_hashing harness: random alphanumeric string keys (length 1-8 or exactly 8; 1-32 and 1-1024 keys) known at compile time, size x 100,000 lookups from a pre-built vector with 100%, 50% or 0% hits (misses are runs of '.'), total time per binary (median of 3 runs, checksums asserted equal across targets); gperf generated with %compare-strncmp, %language=C++, %enum, %readonly-tables, %global-table, %struct-type and --multiple-iterations=1. Secondary: the qlibs/mph README nanobench tables (5, 6 or 100 random-string keys, ns per lookup) and Kronuz/constexpr-phf's string-dispatch benchmark on Xapiand's 192 field-type names.
corrections.claimed_speedup: GNU gperf's own manual and README give no lookup numbers; all numbers are third-party. (1) qlibs/mph perfect_hashing harness on an i7-12650H, plotted total time for size x 100,000 lookups, values read off the notebook's plots (derived from page data, about +/-0.01 s): 1024 string keys of length 1-8, all hits: std::unordered_map ~2.14 s vs gperf ~0.46 s, ~4.7x ('clang++-19' panel), ~2.06 s vs ~0.48 s, ~4.3x ('g++-13' panel), i.e. ~21 ns vs ~4.5 ns per lookup; 1024 keys of length exactly 8, all hits: ~1.58 s vs ~0.32 s, ~4.9x (~1.62 vs ~0.33 s in the other panel); 1024 keys of length 1-8, all misses: ~0.66 s vs ~0.11 s, ~6x (~0.70 vs ~0.11 s); 32 keys of length 1-8, all hits: ~0.052 s vs ~0.0125 s, ~4x ('clang++-19') and ~0.049 vs ~0.010 s, ~5x ('g++-13'). In the same harness mph is about 2-3x faster than gperf on hits (~0.15 s at 1024 keys), while gperf edges mph on 1024-key all-miss runs (~0.11 s vs ~0.13 s). (2) qlibs/mph README nanobench tables, ns/op gperf vs std::unordered_map (boost::hash): clang++: 5 keys len 4 7.70 vs 5.56 (gperf 1.38x slower), 5 len 8 7.70 vs 13.45 (1.75x faster), 6 len 2-5 7.94 vs 15.28 (1.92x), 100 len 8 8.04 vs 15.32 (1.91x), 100 len 1-8 13.06 vs 19.34 (1.48x); g++: 5 len 4 7.69 vs 5.29 (gperf 1.45x slower), 5 len 8 7.92 vs 13.36 (1.69x), 6 len 2-5 9.13 vs 17.56 (1.92x), 100 len 8 7.75 vs 15.01 (1.94x), 100 len 1-8 11.20 vs 25.35 (2.26x) (ratios derived from page data). (3) Kronuz/constexpr-phf README, 192 Xapiand field-type names: gperf 14 ns/op vs std::unordered_map 29 ns/op (2.07x, derived from page data) and std::set 82 ns/op; gperf is the fastest row there, ahead of constexpr-phf (18-21 ns).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: perfect_hashing harness: notebook CXXFLAGS -std=c++20 -DNDEBUG -O3 -march=native, plus -fconstexpr-steps=1000000000 -ftemplate-depth=1024 from the Makefile; panels are labelled clang++-19 and g++-13, but the Makefile hard-codes CXX=clang++-18, which overrides the CXX environment variable the notebook passes, so both panels were most likely built with clang++-18; gperf version not stated (the Dockerfile does not install it). README tables: clang++ and g++ (versions not stated), -std=c++20 -O3 -DNDEBUG -mbmi2. constexpr-phf: GCC 11, -O3, x86_64.
corrections.hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i7-12650H (notebook /proc/cpuinfo), pinned with taskset to logical CPU 1, Turbo Boost on, intel_pstate powersave governor (pyperf system tune output); the README tables state no CPU, and constexpr-phf says only x86_64.
corrections.caveats: All evidence is third-party and comes from competing perfect-hash libraries (qlibs/mph, Kronuz/constexpr-phf), both of which also show their own library beating gperf on hits. The perfect_hashing harness's compiler labels are unreliable (Makefile hard-codes clang++-18; identical binaries in both panels per the wave1-phf qlibs/mph record), the machine ran with turbo on and the powersave governor, the plots must be read off pixels, the 1024-key runs stream a size x 100,000 lookup vector (~100M string_views) so per-lookup times may sit near a memory floor, and the misses are runs of '.' that gperf rejects on length or its first table probe, so the all-miss rows are cheap rather than adversarial. In the README nanobench tables the std::unordered_map baseline uses boost::hash (benchmark/benchmark.cpp), the gperf output is pasted into lambdas and edited to return an index, and gperf loses to std::unordered_map on 5 four-character keys (1.4x slower with both compilers). The qlibs.github.io page carrying the same plots is blocked here; the notebook and its embedded plots were read through raw.githubusercontent.com. libstdc++ is inferred (Ubuntu jammy Docker image, no -stdlib flag). Schmidt's 1990 USENIX C++ paper 'GPERF: A Perfect Hash Function Generator' was not reachable. gperf's output is not under the GPL (manual section 'The Copyright of the Output'): generated tables take the licence of the keyword input, so the GPL-3.0-or-later licence covers the generator only. The repo URL is an unofficial GitHub mirror (0 stars) that stops at gperf 3.2 (last commit 2022-02-08); WebSearch snippets (snippet only) show upstream releases 3.2.1 and 3.3 (3.3 packaged by IPFire in a patch dated 2025-05-24, NEWS: gperf itself 2-2.5x faster), so the mirror lags GNU Savannah, which is blocked here. Not a minimal perfect hash for large key sets: gperf targets small keyword sets and its tables keep empty slots (e.g. 5 keys in an 8-slot table in the README harness).

notes: Numbers in the record match the qlibs/mph README and constexpr-phf README (record omitted three g++ rows, now added). Tier raised C to A on the qlibs/mph perfect_hashing harness (public code, i7-12650H, -O3 -march=native), consistent with qlibs/mph's own A; shortcomings to record: third-party evidence from competitors only, unreliable compiler labels, plot-read values, gperf slower than std::unordered_map on 5 four-character keys, README baseline uses boost::hash, mirror repo lags upstream 3.3. Category: gperf is a static keyword-table generator, not a large-set MPHF, so it fits wave1-phf's perfect-hash-static-tables (frozen, qlibs/mph, constexpr-phf, triehash), where it is the de facto incumbent that triehash, strager/perfect-hash-tables and rurban/perfect-hash benchmark against; consider a category override and a repo_url override to https://www.gnu.org/software/gperf/ (the seed id). maintenance_status left 'unknown': the mirror's last commit is 2022-02-08 (abandoned by the rule), but upstream had a 3.3 release in 2025 per snippets only; git.savannah.gnu.org and sources.debian.org were EGRESS_BLOCKED.
